analysis.one_liner: Imposes a near-total tax on bonuses and stock profits bank executives took out just before their failed bank was seized.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After Silicon Valley Bank and other banks failed in March 2023, reports surfaced that executives had collected large bonuses and sold bank stock shortly before the FDIC took their banks over. This bill would tax those specific bonuses and stock profits at 90% to 100% for executives earning over $250,000, and states that the money should go back into the Deposit Insurance Fund that protects depositors. It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers, by refilling the FDIC's Deposit Insurance Fund — the fund that pays customers back when a bank fails — with money clawed back from executives of failed banks, rather than leaving those costs with other banks and ultimately the public.

how_it_helps.text: It imposes a surtax of 90% to 100% on bonuses paid and stock-sale profits earned by executives of failed banks in the 60 days before the FDIC took the bank over, as long as the executive's income exceeds $250,000.
It states the sense of Congress that the money collected should be returned to the Deposit Insurance Fund, the fund that protects ordinary depositors when banks fail.

analysis.who_pays: Executives of failed banks who collected bonuses or sold bank stock in the two months before their bank was seized, and who earn over $250,000.

drawbacks.text: The top rate reaches 100% on stock-sale profits by executives of failed banks, an unusually steep rate that critics would call punitive and that could be challenged as arbitrary or confiscatory.

The tax is narrow — it reaches only bonuses paid and stock sold within 60 days before a failure, by executives with income above $250,000 — so it would not recover much of the broader cost of a bank failure borne by the FDIC and other banks.
The statement that revenue 'will be returned to the Deposit Insurance Fund' is a sense of Congress, not a binding mechanism, so the money could in practice go to general Treasury purposes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — recapturing executive payouts from failed banks and refilling the insurance fund that protects depositors — is targeted and real, and the cost falls entirely on a small group of well-paid executives rather than taxpayers or bank customers. The drawback is fairness at the edges: a 100% rate on stock sales is close to confiscatory and could be challenged as arbitrary, and the tax is narrow enough that most of the cost of future bank failures would remain with the FDIC and the banking system.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there without ever getting a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the DEPOSIT Act on March 17, 2023, shortly after the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank.
The bill's only action after introduction was referral to the House Ways and Means Committee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives of failed banks keep the bonuses and stock profits they collected before their banks were seized, and taxpayers' Deposit Insurance Fund gets nothing back.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Failed-bank executives; the insurance fund got nothing

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in response to executive bonuses and stock sales before the 2023 bank failures.

for.name: 27 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 27 were Democrats.

against.name: Financial industry and anti-tax groups
against.what_they_did: Financial industry groups have generally opposed retroactive and targeted tax increases on bank compensation, and the Ways and Means Committee leadership declined to act on the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled House Ways and Means Committee.

industries.note: The bill's entire target: it would claw back bonuses and stock profits these executives took out in the two months before their bank was seized, at a 90-100% tax rate. It never passed, so they keep the money.

The surtax applies only to executives of banks that actually fail, so healthy banks pay nothing, but the industry as a whole benefits from the failure of the bill because executive payout practices at failing banks remain untaxed.

The bill would route the collected revenue to the fund that insures depositors, replenishing money spent cleaning up bank failures. That is a public fund, not a private industry, and it never received the money.
